item.title: Nvidia hires major US law firm to investigate alleged Chinese spy affair
item.description:
Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption,
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has become the face of the US AI boomByKali Hays, Technology reporter and Lily Jamali, North America Technology correspondentPublished10 November 2026
Nvidia has hired one of the largest law firms in the US to investigate the affair between its own chief executive and an alleged Chinese spy.
Jensen Huang, who co-founded the tech company, has admitted to having a romantic relationship outside of his marriage. The woman, Alice Huang, is alleged to be a spy for Beijing.
Nvidia said on Tuesday that it had hired New York law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, and that its attorney Joon Kim would lead "a thorough and independent investigation". The FBI is also conducting its own probe.
The company's share price has fallen almost to a yearly low, with $500bn (£375bn) wiped of its stock market value since Friday.
Nvidia is widely considered one of the most important companies behind the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, given it is the sole manufacturer of a computer chip used in AI tools.
It is the world's second most valuable company after Apple and its chips have become a matter of national security for US officials who are keen to win the AI race.
Alice Huang, who is also known as Huang Le, and is not related to Jensen Huang, was an executive at Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has been a customer of Nvidia.
Megaspeed had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China, a concern that Nvidia has said was investigated and debunked.
Nvidia has also maintained that the US government did not inform it that Megaspeed posed an intelligence concern.

item.title: What we know as pressure builds on embattled Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang
item.description:

Watch: Jensen Huang's future at Nvidia 'doesn't look good', the BBC's Lily Jamali explainsByLily Jamali, North America Technology correspondent and Peter Hoskins, Business reporterPublished9 November 2026Updated 2 hours ago
One of the Artificial Intelligence (AI) industry's most important figures could be ousted from his role amid allegations that he had extramarital affairs with two women - one a suspected Chinese spy and the other a company executive.
Chip-maker Nvidia hired a major law firm earlier this week to investigate CEO Jensen Huang's reported relationship with a woman who was allegedly a Chinese intelligence asset.
Now the firm is reportedly weighing whether to remove Huang after its stocks plummeted on Wednesday following US media reports about a second alleged affair.
Huang admitted, external earlier this week to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and he apologised for hurting her and their children.
Here is what we know about the affair and why it matters.
Will Huang be replaced?
Nvidia's board was reportedly meeting on Wednesday evening to decide whether its CEO should remain with the company.
The BBC called Nvidia representatives and board members for comment, but received no reply.
Nvidia has 11 directors on its board, including Huang, and the CEO can be removed with or without cause by a majority vote of directors, according to Reuters news agency.
Should Nvidia's board choose to oust Huang, or place him on leave, it was not immediately clear who might step into his shoes, even on an interim basis.
One possibility is Nvidia co-founder Chris Malachowsky. He has been at the company as long as Huang, and for years led its product engineering work.

item.title: Acquitted 'China spy' tells BBC: I was fall guy for security services but also naive
item.description:
To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.
This video can not be playedFigure caption,
Watch: Chris Cash says counter-terror officers entered his bedroom and arrested himByJoe Pike, politics investigations correspondent and Phil Kemp, politics reporterPublished11 November 2026
A British man who was charged with spying for China has told the BBC he was a "convenient fall guy" for UK police and security services who wanted to put espionage threats by foreign states "on the map".
Chris Cash, a former parliamentary researcher, has shared more than 6,000 messages with us revealing how a Chinese official sought information about sensitive political matters in the UK - including the 2022 Tory leadership battle to decide the next prime minister.
The messages show how Cash's friend in China, Chris Berry - with whom he had been sharing information - dramatically described a "secret" meeting between Berry and a high-ranking Chinese official.
Berry said he had been told that China was concerned about how a British MP it had sanctioned might be promoted to a cabinet role.
The messages also reveal how Cash used his friend as a reference during vetting for a parliamentary pass - which was approved.
Like Cash, Berry was also charged with espionage. The two men consistently maintained their innocence.
In Cash's first interview since his acquittal, which sparked a political row over the government's failure to designate China as a "threat", he says he would "never do anything" to harm UK national security.
But he admits he was "unprofessional and naive" to send "gossiping" texts to his friend, whom he met in 2018 when they both taught English in a school in China.
Although the trove of messages shows him discussing sensitive topics, there is no evidence in them that Cash was paid by, or sympathetic to, the Chinese Communist Party.

item.title: He spent $50,000 on Labubus but now the craze is dying
item.description:
Image source, Courtesy of EnsitoImage caption,
Ensito, with his custom-made Labubu teeth, posing with a new doll in his collection ByOsmond ChiaBusiness reporterPublished7 November 2026
For years, Labubu dolls seemed unstoppable.
Collectors young and old energetically snapped up "blind boxes" - sealed, mystery packages containing the quirky monsters - often paying $15 (£11) or more.
Those unable to get the characters they wanted were often prepared to pay much more on the resale market.
The hype around the creatures convinced a mega-fan from North Carolina, who goes by the name Ensito, to leave his tech job in 2024 to create Labubu content full-time, travelling as far as Italy and Spain to seek out the latest releases.
Ensito has spent more than $50,000 (£37,000) to build his collection of more than 400 Labubus, a figure he tells the BBC he's "embarrassed to say".
He even had a row of custom Labubu-like jagged teeth made by a dentist to wear at events.
But in recent months, Ensito's once-viral posts about the furry monsters have struggled. "Those videos used to be able to hit 10,000 really quickly but I'm struggling to do that now."
Ensito's focus has shifted to other trends like Hello Kitty and squishies.
It's a sign that the craze which made parent company Pop Mart worth more than US toy giants Hasbro and Mattel put together may be running out of steam. Analysts believe the Beijing-based brand is struggling to capture excitement beyond a single viral moment.
Pop Mart recently reported that global sales in the three months to the end of September had fallen by as much as 50% on the previous year.
The drop was particularly steep outside mainland China, with US revenue down by at least 70%.
Image source, Reuters
The rise and fall
Pop Mart didn't invent blind boxes but its dolls certainly helped to popularise them around the world.

item.description:

Watch: Hong Kong pro-democracy advocate Joshua Wong jailed for 10 yearsByAbel U, BBC Chinese, Reporting fromHong Kong and Kelly NgPublished5 November 2026
Joshua Wong, once the face of Hong Kong's democracy movement, has been sentenced to 10 years in jail for colluding with foreign forces under the city's sweeping national security law.
Wong is among hundreds of campaigners and ordinary Hongkongers arrested under the law, which was imposed in 2020 following explosive pro-democracy protests against Beijing's growing control.
Critics say the far-reaching law has silenced dissent, but authorities argue that it is needed to maintain stability and deny it has weakened the city's cherished autonomy.
Having already spent the last six years in jail, Wong, who was due to be freed in January, will now spend another decade behind bars.
Silenced and erased, Hong Kong's decade of protest is now a defiant memory
Published30 November 2024

On Thursday, he arrived in court wearing a dark blue long-sleeved shirt, khaki trousers and black-rimmed glasses. He looked slimmer compared to his previous public appearances.
He nodded in greeting towards members of the packed public gallery, and took notes intermittently as the judge read out the reasons for his sentencing.
A crowd had gathered outside the court, with dozens of Hongkongers having queued for hours hoping to get a seat in the public gallery. There was also a heavy police presence.
Wong is already serving time for subversion and was due to be freed early next year when he was handed the latest charges, to which he pleaded guilty in September.

item.title: Weapon or wine bottle? China disputes reports of artillery shell in Papua New Guinea
item.description:
Image source, PNG East New Britain Province Facebook pageImage caption,
The 32kg object was found at a construction site in Port MoresbyByKelly NgPublished4 November 2026
Chinese authorities have dismissed reports that a suspected China-made artillery shell was found in a commercial shipping container in Papua New Guinea, saying it is a "shell-shaped wine bottle".
"It poses no danger at all," the Chinese embassy wrote in a Facebook post on Tuesday, drawing sceptical comments.
Police in Port Moresby arrested four Chinese nationals last Friday after the 32kg object was found at a construction site in the capital city.
Authorities were looking into whether it was a live device, local reports said then, with police commissioner David Manning describing it as "a very concerning discovery".
In a report on Wednesday, the Australia Broadcasting Corporation cited unnamed sources identifying the object as an undetonated 130mm Chinese Type 59 Artillery Projectile that contains chemical explosives and a fuse. The BBC has not independently verified this.
Papua New Guinea police had earlier dismissed speculation that the object was "merely a dummy", local newspaper Post Courier said.
However, the Chinese embassy said in its statement that it is "virtually impossible" for an illegal military-grade artillery shell to be smuggled out of China to Papua New Guinea.
"China enforces some of the world's strictest firearm control laws and regulations," it wrote, adding that China is "widely recognised as one of the safest countries globally".
Some Facebook users appear unconvinced.
"What sort of wine bottle weighs 32 kilograms?" wrote one of them.
Another wrote that the object bore no labels indicating that it's a wine bottle.

item.title: Crypto giant Binance hit by $6.3bn hack suspected to be largest in history
item.description:
Image source, VCG/VCG via Getty ImagesByOsmond Chia, Business reporter and Angus ThompsonPublished30 October 2026
Cryptocurrency giant Binance said on Thursday that $6.3bn (£4.7bn) of digital assets have been impacted by what is thought to be the biggest crypto hack on record.
The world's biggest crypto exchange said about half of those assets had been frozen but that many remained in the hands of the hackers, adding that it will "cover all losses".
The firm said while initial checks suggested an engineer's laptop had been compromised, allowing an attacker to make unauthorised withdrawals, "our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach".
Two analytics firms have attributed the incident, which eclipses a record-setting $1.5bn hack on the Bybit exchange in 2025, to a North Korean hacking unit called TraderTraitor.
Cyber-security firm Check Point said the unit is also known in the industry as Lazarus Group, which has been blamed for the 2025 hack.
Check Point's chief information security officer Jayant Dave said the losses estimated by Binance made it "the largest crypto theft on record".
AI-powered investigations company TRM Labs said in a report that several elements of the Binance attack resemble earlier North Korean-linked incidents, including the Bybit hack.
The lab's global head of policy Ari Redbord told the BBC the Binance hack is a "watershed moment" that is unlike anything the industry has seen.
The attacker still holds an enormous sum of stolen assets, meaning efforts to trace and recover the funds are far from over, Redbord added.
Binance, which was founded in China in 2017, allows users to trade digital assets and is estimated to have more than 300 million registered users worldwide.
The company said in 2024 that it has more than $160bn in assets under its custody.
The exchange has been subject of regulatory scrutiny around the world.

item.title: Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond
item.description:
Image source, ReutersImage caption,
Jensen Huang, 63, has been called the 'Taylor Swift of tech' in the USByZoe Kleinman
Technology and AI editorPublished9 November 2026
The tech world has spent the day digesting the extraordinary news that Jensen Huang - the charismatic, leather-jacket wearing chief executive of the multi-trillion dollar firm Nvidia - is being investigated by his own company over an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.
None of us had that on our bingo cards for 2026.
Huang's alleged romantic affair with Alice Huang (no relation), the former CEO of a Singapore-based data centre company, has cast ripples far beyond his immediate family - undoubtedly on an emotional rollercoaster of their own - taking us to a crossroads at which technology, geopolitics and national security intersect.
In a nutshell, this is about the bitter rivalry between the US and China, as well as whether Jensen Huang has betrayed the US as well as his wife.

"Whoever wins AI, wins," as US President Donald Trump puts it. He thinks that the country with the more dominant AI technology will benefit the most from it and, ultimately, will be the most powerful in the world. He may well be right.

item.title: China's families are now supporting more old people than kids
item.description:
Image source, VCG via Getty ImagesByOsmond ChiaBusiness reporterPublished27 October 2026
Families in China are for the first time supporting more elderly people than children, the country's government has said.
Official data released in the last week, external show the ratio of China's dependent elderly people compared to the working age population rose to 23% last year, overtaking the figure for children, which stood at 22%.
The numbers are closely watched for signs of how China's shrinking workforce will impact both the world's second largest economy and global growth as a whole.
The latest figures mark a significant milestone as China grapples with an ageing population that could have implications for families, pensions and healthcare spending, analysts say.
China has been preparing for a growing proportion of elderly people in recent years, while urging younger generations to get married and for couples to have more children.
The latest data from China's National Bureau of Statistics show there are now more than 223 million people in China aged 65 and above, accounting for nearly 16% of the country's total population.
At the same time there are about 213 million children aged 14 and under.
No official commentary was published with the statistics. But Chinese state-controlled news outlet Global Times wrote that the nation's "entry into a moderately ageing society" is the result of a mix of factors, including the "size of past birth cohorts" and longer life expectancy.
The shift could place added strain on pension, healthcare and long-term care systems, while also creating opportunities in the so-called silver economy that caters to older consumers, the newspaper said.
"It reflects a historical trend in demographic development rather than a short-term phenomenon," Global Times quoted one researcher as saying.

item.title: China made Mbappé apologise - but many don't know exactly what he said
item.description:
Image source, CFOTO/Future Publishing via Getty ImagesByFan WangPublished29 October 2026
On Monday night, as Kylian Mbappé was attending the Ballon d'Or ceremony in London, he was also becoming the centre of a huge controversy on Chinese social media.
Football fans had stumbled upon a clip of him joking about the meme that makes him "laugh the most" - where his face is superimposed on a "Chinese dictator" resembling Mao Zedong, who oversaw one of the bloodiest chapters in the country's past.
The controversy spread like wildfire as Chinese brands cut him off one by one and China Media Group, the parent group of state broadcaster CCTV, suspended broadcasts of La Liga matches. A foreign ministry spokesperson said: "Words and actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people will naturally be met with joint opposition from all sectors of Chinese society."
But on the Chinese internet, few were explicitly spelling out those words and actions, or even using the name of Mao - who remains a near-sacred figure in the country.
To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.
This video can not be playedFigure caption,
Watch: The Mbappé-Chairman Mao controversy explained
China's sophisticated censorship system, which cuts 1.4 billion people off from the global internet, meant many didn't know exactly what had happened.
The accusation of "hurting the feelings of the Chinese people" alone seemed enough to trigger a tsunami of anger, amplified by social media algorithms and a heavily controlled internet, where people are wary of disagreeing with the majority view.
It wasn't long before Mbappé, one of the biggest football stars in the world, said he was "sincerely sorry" for his "ill-judged" comment. His club, Real Madrid, and the Spanish league La Liga, also issued apologies. China is a huge market for the world's most popular sport.
